projects.tagline: Ant colony optimisation for mobile ad hoc networks: the colony the org grew out of.
summary: AntHocNet (Di Caro, Ducatelle & Gambardella, 2005) routes like a foraging colony. When a data packet finds no route, the source sends **reactive forward ants** that search towards the destination; each one flips into a **backward ant** there and walks the path home, laying pheromone that scores each next hop. The backward ant is the only thing that deposits regular pheromone.

While a session runs, **proactive ants** keep sampling and improving the path, **hello** beacons keep the neighbour set fresh and diffuse a virtual pheromone, and when a link breaks the node sends **repair** ants or a **LinkFail** notification upstream. Data follows the pheromone stochastically, so load spreads over several good paths.

The algorithm is written once, as a simulator-agnostic `core/` (C++23) that takes time, randomness, neighbours and timers through ports. The ns-3 module and the browser adapter only convert headers and carry out the core's `RouteDecision`s; the game here runs that same `core/` compiled to WebAssembly, byte-identical to the native trace.

projects.tagline: The Ant-Colony-Based Routing Algorithm: reactive ants, data that reinforces its own path.
summary: ARA (Güneş, Sorges & Bouazizi, 2002) is the lean ancestor in the family. Route discovery floods a **forward ant (FANT)** from the source; every node it reaches records pheromone back towards the source. The destination answers with a **backward ant (BANT)**, which sets up pheromone towards the destination on the way back.

After discovery there are no maintenance ants: **data packets themselves reinforce** the pheromone of the links they use, and pheromone **evaporates** over time, so unused routes fade. Duplicate packets are detected by sequence number to stop loops, and a broken link makes the node try another next hop before reporting a route error upstream.

Here ARA is a standalone protocol on the org's hexagonal pattern: a fresh simulator-agnostic `core/` on `swarm-core` and the ns-3 module `ara`, which replaces AntHocNet's `ara` comparator arm. The core implements route discovery, data reinforcement, and duplicate errors with route-failure backtracking (§3.2–3.3), reported through swarm-core's router observer; the adapter carries them out.

Of the three comparator gates it clears two: the fidelity sheet, which sources each parameter from the paper or marks it a repository choice, and the per-PR delivery smoke. The third, an anchor reproducing the paper's trend against AODV, **misses**: three pre-registered runs are read in a written infeasibility verdict, with their raw cells in the repository, so ARA's delivery numbers are not presented as a reproduction of the paper. The next anchor is the 2003 version's, a different source with its own trend.

projects.tagline: Honeybee foraging as routing: scouts find paths, foragers carry data along them, the battery decides.
summary: BeeAdHoc (Wedde & Farooq, 2005), here in the version the PG 460 report's Linux kernel module specifies: the only version given down to its constants. When no route is known, **scouts** are broadcast towards the destination with an expanding ring and come back with the path they found. That path becomes a **forager** in a per-destination forager array, and data travels along foragers' source routes.

Each data packet carries a versioned **source-route trailer** (the route, its information and one piggybacked forager); foreign foragers learned on the way are sent home in **swarms**, and a failed link removes every forager whose first hop it is. Routes are rated by the **battery (energy) metric** only, read through swarm-core's `EnergyMetricHook` over `ns3::EnergySource`. The formal model's packers and dance-floor recruitment are out of scope; adding them later would be a default-off mechanism with its own A/B.

Here BeeAdHoc is a standalone protocol on the org's hexagonal pattern: a simulator-agnostic `core/` on `swarm-core`, reported through swarm-core's router observer, and the ns-3 module `beeadhoc`, which carries every decision out. Where the sources disagree, each interpretation is pre-registered in an issue, with its evidence, before code.

Of the three comparator gates it clears two: the fidelity sheet, every row against PG 460's Linux module, and the per-PR delivery smoke. The third, an anchor reproducing the report's control-overhead trend against AODV and DSDV, **misses**: the pre-registered run is read in a written infeasibility verdict, with its raw cells in the repository, so BeeAdHoc's numbers are not presented as a reproduction of the report.

projects.tagline: Routing by stigmergy: the pheromone rides inside the data packets themselves.
summary: Termite (Roth & Wicker; GLOBECOM 2003, SIDM 2005, Roth's 2005 dissertation) has **no control ants**. Every data packet carries routing state: as a packet arrives, the receiving node strengthens its pheromone towards the packet's **source** through the neighbour it came from. Traffic in one direction builds the routes for traffic in the other.

Forwarding is **randomised multipath**: the next hop is drawn in proportion to pheromone, and pheromone **decays** with time, so the table tracks a moving topology without beacons of its own. What a node does with a packet for a destination it holds no pheromone for is one of the questions the fidelity sheet settles from the dissertation.

AntHocNet's Termite arm passed the delivery smoke but missed its anchor in v2.5.0 (trend right, confidence intervals spanning zero). Whether that was the arm, the scenario or statistical power is pre-registered in an issue before `core/` is written.

projects.tagline: Ants that hop between routing zones: proactive inside a zone, reactive between zones.
summary: HOPNET (Wang, 2007 MSc thesis, University of Manitoba) crosses ant colony routing with **zone routing**. Each node keeps a zone of nodes within a few hops. Inside the zone, routes are kept **proactively**; towards a destination outside it, **forward ants hop from zone border to zone border** instead of flooding every node, and backward ants bring the path home.

It is the one published result found that benchmarks against AntHocNet directly, claiming better scaling, so its anchor pairs the two through sim-tools with the AntHocNet configuration pinned and stated. No AntHocNet code exists for it: `core/` is written fresh from the thesis.

projects.tagline: The ns-3 adapter of swarm-core's ports: the swarm-core contrib module every protocol links against.
summary: `swarm-core` is the shared ns-3 contrib module (`libns3.<ver>-swarm-core`, `#include "ns3/swarm-core-module.h"`) every protocol links against: the ns-3 adapter of swarm-core's ports. It has **no `core/` of its own** any more: the simulator-free C++23 primitives (the bounded `VisitedPath`, little-endian wire helpers, `PheromoneTable`, `RouteDecision`, the `ILinkState` / `ILinkMetric` seams, evaporation and roulette selection, the testbench) live in [swarm-core](/projects/swarm-core/), extracted from this repository's `core/` with its history. The module's `CMakeLists.txt` reads `swarm-core.lock`, fetches that swarm-core release's tarball (`FetchContent`, URL and SHA256, `SOURCE_SUBDIR core`) and links its target `swarm::core` to `libswarm-core` as a `PUBLIC` dependency, so a module that links `${libswarm-core}` gets the primitives, their include directory, their C++ standard and their headers as `ns3/swarm-*.h` with no edit of its own.

Its `model/` holds the ns-3 glue: `SwarmRoutingBase` (sockets, deferred routes, node lifecycle, the observer's trace sources), a `DeferredPacketQueue`, `WifiLinkMonitor`, `EnergyMetricHook` over `ns3::EnergySource`, and `IslLinkMonitor` for satellite links; `helper/` installs a protocol in one call. Nothing protocol-specific lands here: code is promoted only when a second protocol needs it.

**v1.0.0 froze the API**: `kSwarmCoreApiVersion` is 2, the module's public API is recorded in `docs/api-surface.txt` and a required `api-surface` check fails a change that removes or alters an item without a breaking mark, and a breaking change waits for a major after a deprecation (`docs/api-policy.md`). **v2.0.0's breaking change is the layout, not the C++ API**: the primitives' names, signatures and headers are unchanged, but `contrib/swarm-core/core/` is gone (a module takes swarm-core's include directory from linking `${libswarm-core}`), `core/` no longer builds from this repository or its release tarball, and the API record keeps the module's ns-3 items only (swarm-core keeps its own). `IslLinkMonitor`, with the base API only it drives, is experimental, outside that promise until a second protocol adopts it. CI runs every org quality gate, the determinism gate included (same seed twice byte-identical, another seed different).

**Renamed from ns3-swarm-core on 2026-11-22** (ROADMAP phase 0): it is layer 2 of the org's four layers, the ns-3 runtime adapter. The contrib module keeps its name `swarm-core`. In phase 1 its simulator-free `core/` moved with its history to [swarm-core](/projects/swarm-core/) ([swarm-adapter-ns3#231](https://github.com/swarm-routing/swarm-adapter-ns3/issues/231)), and swarm-adapter-ns3 now builds on that release (ROADMAP, [Architecture and migration](https://github.com/swarm-routing/.github/blob/main/ROADMAP.md#architecture-and-migration-decided-2026-11-22)).

projects.tagline: Protocol-agnostic comparison: the harness every arm registers with, and the scripts that judge the runs.
summary: sim-tools is where protocols meet on equal terms. The `routing-bench` module (moved from AntHocNet as-is) is the comparison harness: every protocol, ours or a comparator, registers as an **arm** through its own `helper/<module>-bench-arms.cc`, and no arm is special-cased. It also holds the measurement itself today: the topology oracle (BFS-reachable delivery ratio, path stretch) and the drop book (PHY/MAC/ARP/TTL/loop root causes). A run prints the versioned marker lines `##CONFIG##`, `##RUN##`, `##BENCH##`, `##DIAG##`, `##PROV##` and `##PERF##`. Each arm runs in its own process by default (`--isolateArms`), and a run whose simulated time stops advancing, a zero-time event storm like NS3-001, stops after `--livelockEvents` events at one instant instead of running until the job times out.

The `ns3-tool` CLI (`compare`, `sweep`, `diagnose`, `scaffold`) fronts the Python readers (stdlib only): they parse those lines and do the statistics, per-seed paired deltas over at least 20 seeds and a scripted noise verdict, never an eyeballed one, checked byte-identical against fixture cells from AntHocNet. `ns3-campaign` runs a multi-protocol campaign: one image, every cell pulled by digest, each keyed over every pinned input; it also runs a protocol repository's change-test plans, where a never-published smoke plan may name its image by a rolling tag that the first dispatch resolves to a digest the whole campaign keeps. The CLI and marker contract v1 are frozen: fields, commands and options are only appended, and a breaking change waits for contract v2.

Planned next: non-intrusive probes as their own module (the oracle and the drop book extracted), the satellite harnesses on the arm registry, and the non-swarm comparator arms, each its own module under `ns3/arms/`. Whether the universal arenas of the original plan stay is an open decision.

**Renamed from ns3-tools on 2026-11-22** (ROADMAP phase 0). It owns orchestration and statistics for every simulator (ROADMAP decision 24): the simulator-agnostic runner, the seed sweeps, the shared telemetry schema and the statistics; its per-simulator directories hold only launch configs and trace normalizers, never adapter code. The release, the `ns3-tools.lock` pin and PyPI's `ns3-tools` keep their names. It also keeps the org's register of upstream ns-3 bugs (`docs/ns3-bugs.md`, `NS3-NNN`), each with its RCAPA under `docs/ns3-rcapa/`.

projects.tagline: ns-3 pre-built and tested, so a contrib module compiles alone in seconds.
summary: sim-containers publishes `ghcr.io/swarm-routing/ns3-dev` (public, no login): ns-3 configured and built with Ninja at `/opt/ns-3`. A downstream module is linked into the warm tree by `ns3-build-contrib` and compiles alone; the smoke gate counts the Ninja steps (8 today, gate 40) to prove the cache was hit.

Automatic pipelines build only the release ns-3 supports (its latest), read from upstream's tags by `tools/ns3_matrix.py`, never a hand-typed version. Older releases are built on demand and kept as history. Four profiles: `default`, `debug` (CI), `sanitized` (ASan + LSan + UBSan) and `optimized` (ns-3's `release`, for campaigns only, never `-march=native`).

**What is tested is what is tagged:** each image is built once, every test stage runs on that build by digest (structure, profile, smoke, integration, unit, Trivy security), and the published tags are a carbon copy of that digest, then signed and attested. A published number pins the immutable `:<ver>-<profile>-<sha7>` tag.

The image pipeline itself is versioned: a release archives the Dockerfile, `ns3-build-contrib`, the test stages and `tools/` at a commit, while an image tag stays the ns-3 release it was built from. Before a `latest-*` tag moves, the downstream canary builds and tests every org module on the new image.

**Renamed from ns3-containers on 2026-11-22** (ROADMAP phase 0); the image keeps its name `ghcr.io/swarm-routing/ns3-dev`. Other simulators' images follow ns-3 and Linux parity (ROADMAP decision 8), deferred with the simulator track (decision 23).

A port downloads a published release asset and checks it by SHA512; a release of the library opens the bump PR here, and `tools/port_bump.py` writes the bump and each port's description from its upstream repository. A protocol core waits in `templates/` until its repository's first release installs `core/` as a CMake package, then moves into `ports/`. The ns-3 modules are not ports, and the org's own repositories take swarm-core by release lock, not through this registry.

projects.tagline: The org's bridge to ns-3's GitLab: a mirror ticket per upstream bug report, with no manual step.
summary: When the org finds a bug in ns-3 itself (an `NS3-NNN` entry of sim-tools' register), this repository carries the report upstream to [ns-3's GitLab](https://gitlab.com/nsnam/ns-3-dev): one **mirror ticket** per report, the GitLab notes and state mirrored back, the text sent only from merged files (`reports/`, `replies/`), every guard of the bridge checked before each GitLab call, and a veto window (the `hold` label) in place of approvals. The register and the root-cause records stay in sim-tools.

Every pipeline is one Go tool, `cmd/upstream`: `read` mirrors GitLab every 6 h, `send` posts a merged report or reply, `verify` re-runs each reproducer weekly on ns-3-dev master, `lifecycle` follows a fix into an ns-3 release, `maintain` keeps a merge request rebased, `rotate` renews the token. Only `internal/gitlabwrite` writes to GitLab, and only `send`, `maintain` and `rotate` import it: the read side cannot write. `tracked.toml` is the allowlist; nothing is posted for an item it does not list.

projects.tagline: The org's MCP server: local, read-only, each tool one command of an org script, its summary capped.
summary: swarm-mcp is a local, read-only [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server (stdio, Python stdlib) whose tools each run one read-only command of a `swarm-routing/.github` script: a fidelity sheet's checks, the golden-rule checks on a diff, a release's readiness and aftercare, a release lock. Each returns the script's own summary, capped; exit 1 means findings.

The Claude Code plugin `swarm-routing` from swarm-routing/skills starts it at the commit its `swarm-mcp.lock` pins; any other MCP client runs it the same way. Skills hold the procedures, this repository the server, each versioned and released on its own. Every tool's schema is closed and no argument can start with `-`; the server runs a fixed table of commands, never a shell, opens no connection and reads no token.

projects.tagline: The org's agent skills: one Claude Code plugin and plain Agent Skills for any agent, each a procedure over an org script.
summary: skills publishes the organisation's agent skills two ways from one tree: as the Claude Code plugin `swarm-routing` (marketplace `swarm-routing`, enabled from each org repository's committed `.claude/settings.json`), and as plain [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/specification) that [skills.sh](https://skills.sh) installs into any agent with `npx skills add swarm-routing/skills`.

Each skill is a procedure over a script in `swarm-routing/.github` `tools/` (or this repository's own `tools/`), script first: the script does the work and runs without the skill, the skill says when and in what order. The plugin also bundles swarm-mcp, the org's read-only MCP server, at the commit `swarm-mcp.lock` pins, and a one-repository subagent, `org-worker`. A merged skill runs with the permissions of every session that enables the marketplace, so every change is a reviewed pull request.
